status: alternative draft only; not reader content; not additional coverage
reason: Repository gained these increments during this turn; canonical earlier English preserved verbatim.

entries.english: He says in al-Nafaḥāt: ‘At this station there is no affirmation of unity opposed by overt or hidden association, nor any unity opposed by multiplicity. Rather, the matter is a reality from which intelligible unity and multiplicity arise—indeed, unity and multiplicity as prescribed by revelation and as witnessed as well. Its unity is its very multiplicity, and its simplicity its very composition. Manifestation and concealment are two states of this reality, determined for our faculties of perception according to the circumstances. Diversification in all its kinds is intrinsic to it and inseparable from it. Stability belongs to the states considered in their realities, not to the One who appears and becomes determined through them.’ Thus far his words.

Since both considerations are required by that Reality, the realised knower who has actualised his vicegerency of God must give each possessor of a right its due. He says that the purpose served by obligation, on the side of the Real and Reality, is the manifestation of His rank as the Worshipped; on the side of the locus of manifestation and the creature, it is that, when they recognise their necessary choice and their real incapacity, they may see that their outward action, relative perfection and otherworldly recompense proceed solely from the reality of divine generosity.
entries.notes: ‘Necessary choice’ (الاختيار الضروري) is explained in §4.954 as ontological dependence, distinguished from compulsion in §4.955.

entries.english: The Great Shaykh—may God be pleased with him—apparently indicated this in that same introduction, when he went on to say: ‘I thank Him with the thanks of one who has realised that through obligation the Name “the Worshipped” becomes manifest, and through the reality of “There is no power and no strength except through God” the attribute of generosity becomes manifest. Otherwise, if you make Paradise a recompense for what you have done, where is the divine generosity you have conceived? You are veiled from knowing that your very self is a gift, and from knowing the origin of your soul. If that by which you seek recompense does not belong to you, how can you regard your action as your own? Leave things to their Creator and those who receive provision to their Provider.’ Thus far his words.
entries.notes: Continues the quotation from Ibn ʿArabī’s Futūḥāt introduction begun in the preceding increment; punctuation is editorial.

entries.english: I say: Combining the two considerations is the intention of those who ascribe action to the Real as creation and to creatures as acquisition, explaining acquisition as the action’s attribution to its recipient through a choice, even though that choice is necessary. Such are the People of the Sunna, especially the Ḥanafī Māturīdīs—may God multiply their like. This accords with the outward convention of Arabic, which regards attributing actions to their recipients as literal. Obligation is therefore valid, and outward requitals, such as retaliation, follow from those actions, even though the dead person was killed at his appointed term. It also accords with the inward understanding of Reality: that choice is a ray or a necessary effect of the universal, unitary choice belonging to the Real—indeed, a subtle thread of it. This is what its inward necessity, as distinct from outward necessity, means, and what is meant by his being killed at his appointed term. Yet the ruling of every reality appears in a locus according to that locus’s preparedness and the state determining it. Similarly, otherworldly recompenses outwardly correspond to voluntary actions belonging to loci of manifestation. Inwardly, agreeable recompenses proceed solely from the Real’s kindness and generosity, whereas disagreeable ones proceed from His justice, founded upon the locus’s insufficient receptivity to something better. This is the meaning of his saying, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, ‘People are recompensed according to their deeds …’; and, ‘Whoever finds good, let him praise God; whoever finds otherwise, let him blame only himself’; and, ‘All good is in Your hands, and evil is not attributed to You’; and similar sayings.
entries.notes: The source explicitly praises the Ḥanafī Māturīdīs. Preserve creation/acquisition, inward/outward necessity, and attribution/receptivity as distinct considerations. The reports are translated as cited; independent hadith verification is pending.

entries.english: As for the doctrine of compulsion, it takes no account whatsoever of the possible human being as a locus of manifestation. It is refuted by the self-evident difference between such things as falling and descending.
entries.notes: The contrast is involuntary falling versus an agent’s descent; the author rejects jabr here.

entries.english: As for the doctrine of independent power, it takes no account of real Oneness and the particular face. This is my understanding, and God knows best.

We now say: One sign of a person who knows through unveiling, rather than through cleverness, these principles establishing the Oneness of the Essence and of action in everything is that he experiences a bewilderment whose removal he neither expects nor entertains doubts about, and which he cannot dispel. Unveiling brings the witnessing of Oneness and the particular face. Once this witnessing becomes a firmly rooted disposition—which is the intended goal—the bewilderment arising from the rulings of multiplicity, such as the obligation to worship, cannot be removed, as appeared in the Great Shaykh’s verses. Whenever that bewilderment is absent, knowledge of these principles is not experiential, but remains behind the veil of manifestation. Another sign is realising that no thing has, in the reality of the matter itself, a fixed intelligible or sensible form except in relation to some degree, state, or perceiver, according to a faculty, attribute or instrument. An indication of this is that intelligible forms differ with intellects in strength, sharpness, subtlety and soundness.

Some intelligible forms cannot be opposed by the estimative faculties, whereas others can; this disparity is the source of disagreement concerning intelligibles. As for sensibles, sense apprehends substances only by sensing accidents and by the intellect’s judgement that these have a substrate. Substantiality may therefore be the relation constituted by the gathering of accidents, as the Illuminationists held. Some theologians also maintained that indivisible substances are homogeneous; on that account, differences between the realities of bodies arise through differences in their accidents. As for accidents, they do not persist for two moments, and so cannot be encompassed by sensible pointing, especially those that are not stable. For, according to the principle of realisation, accidents are forms of determinate relations dependent upon substantial relations. Every instant undoubtedly contributes to their determination, as the Exalted says: ‘Every day He is upon a task’ (Qurʾān 55:29)—that is, every instant, as explained earlier. The relation is renewed with the instants, and so is its form; indeed, so is the relation of substantiality, especially if it is constituted by accidental relations. This is indicated by His saying: ‘Rather, they are in confusion concerning a new creation’ (Qurʾān 50:15). If they are renewed at every instant, sensible pointing cannot fix them, and the senses therefore do not apprehend them.
entries.notes: The witness has فلانا لا تبقى where the argument requires ‘because they do not persist’; Arabic is preserved. These are historical metaphysical and epistemological arguments, not experimental findings.

entries.english: We then say: If it is asked, ‘To what does “the reality of the matter itself” (nafs al-amr) pertain, and what is actually established within it?’
entries.notes: The Arabic question فيما يتعلق نفس الامر is syntactically compressed; this translation takes it as a question about the scope and content of nafs al-amr.

entries.english: I reply: The totality of matters and judgements whose nature is to differ with differences in intellectual apprehension, if they are intelligible, and with differences in witnessed apprehension, if they are sensible—whether they obtain in a given relation or do not obtain in that relation. This is what the knower of God intended when, asked what the Real intends by creation, he said: ‘What they are upon.’ Most people suppose this to be clear, but it is not: they are accustomed to counting renewed likenesses as the persistence of the first thing, especially in bodies. The intellect may be brought to recognise this through the foregoing explanation concerning substance and accident.
entries.notes: The clause إذا سأل … فيما قال is unstable in the electronic witness; the question-and-answer reading is provisional. No silent Arabic repair has been made.

entries.english: This position receives support from the arguments of the Sophists who deny the realities of things, as recorded in the theoretical sciences. Their error, however, lies in denying the Essence. These relations—substantiality, accidentality, celestiality, elementality and others—are attributes of the essence of the unitary existential self-disclosure, eternal without beginning or end, whose relations are renewed with every recipient, as established. Those relations are the realities of the Names under one consideration, and cosmic realities under another.
We now say: Among the signs of this experiential taste—that is, the taste of contemplating the Oneness of the Essence of Being and the particular face—are the following.

First, its possessor does not grieve over something missed, even if what has occurred is the less desirable of two things according to his judgement, temperament, state, abode or rank. He knows that the apparent reason for that preference is a matter of consideration: what seems less desirable may be more desirable under another consideration, or several others. As the Exalted says: ‘It may be that you dislike something while it is good for you …’ (Qurʾān 2:216). And it has been said: ‘Fear when you rise hopeful, and hope when you rise afraid: many a hated, dreaded thing contains good and subtle kindnesses.’
entries.notes: The source introduces the verse with فعسى; the English conveys the cited sense. The two-line verse’s attribution remains unidentified.

entries.english: Or this is because it is purely the act of the Real, who is the source of every good, and He chose it for some good; or because the contrary of what has occurred is impossible, and there is no grief over missing the impossible. Rather, we say, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, said: ‘Had it been decreed, it would have happened.’
entries.notes: ولخير ما اختاره is read as ‘He chose it for some good’. The report is translated as attributed, without independent authentication.

entries.english: Second, he does not give himself to regret or declare of a particular thing [that he will do it], as the Exalted says: ‘Do not say of anything, “I shall do that tomorrow,” except [by adding], “If God wills”’ (Qurʾān 18:23–24). The matter is in God’s hand: what is decreed may be its contrary, in which case it cannot occur.
entries.notes: The bracket supplies the content of ولا يقول على شئ بعينه from the following Qurʾānic citation. This passage is part of the description of a spiritual standpoint, alongside the earlier affirmation of obligation.

entries.english: Third, he does not yearn to attain some particular object, whether relatively noble or otherwise, or exert contrived effort to obtain it. Such effort contains a claim to power for oneself, which is incompatible with witnessing Oneness and the particular face—unless the moment determines it; that is, unless the divine incoming inspiration determines it in accordance with the circumstances mentioned below. This is a discontinuous exception, meaning ‘but’: the object may be determined by his time, as when bedtime calls for somewhere to sleep; by his state, as when intending ablution calls for suitable water, or hunger for something to satisfy it; by his temperament, as when some treatment is required, even through food, drink or rest; by his place, since mosques call for acts of worship rather than commercial transactions; or by the rank in which he has been established, as the rank of spiritual guidance calls for what will set the disciples’ condition right. In this sense the Sufi is the child of his moment, although the perfected person is the father of his moment. Acting upon what the divine incoming inspiration determines is the rank of proximity through supererogatory acts, according to the saying: ‘Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, and through Me he strikes.’ The people of outward understanding take this to mean that in every action he has in view an aspect directed toward God, as Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ mentions in al-Shifāʾ: some aspect of worship, even in permissible things. Thus one eats intending to gain strength for obedience; marries intending to lower one’s gaze and increase the number of worshippers; leaves home intending to look with a view to taking a lesson, to enjoin right and forbid wrong, or to seek what enables obedience; and returns home intending to maintain family ties or withdraw for worship, and so forth.
entries.notes: تعَمّل is rendered as contrived effort because the passage immediately allows action required by concrete circumstances, bodily needs, and responsibilities. The wording of the proximity report is retained as cited.

entries.english: Fourth, he is not affected in his entirety by a particular matter. If affected at all, he is affected in certain respects by certain events: perhaps that matter will not produce the anticipated effect, or something will intervene to prevent it. Alternatively, contemplation of Oneness makes the occurrence something from himself to himself, rather than from another. This latter account is more appropriate and fitting.

Fifth, he sees no disparity in the cosmos, either within himself or outside himself. There is no disparity in what the one Reality requires insofar as it is required by that Reality; or the disparity belongs to the multiplicities that have been effaced from his contemplation. Rather, he sees all occurring forms as related to the uniquely One Essence in the way that Zayd’s limbs are related to his determinate reality.

Sixth, he does not judge the degrees to be independently actualised existents, but relative matters without weight [in this contemplation]. That is why we have said that we fear the possessor of this taste may cease to honour the degrees. Nor does he judge an existent to have such-and-such a rank, since that judgement belongs to his own perspective: it may in fact be higher or lower. Related to this is what is transmitted in the revealed Law: one should not judge a person to be among the people of Paradise or the people of the Fire, except someone explicitly designated by the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him and his family—such as the Ten Given Glad Tidings—or by his inheritors.
entries.notes: The warning about ceasing to honour ranks is Fanārī’s own qualification, not a recommendation to disregard them. ‘Or by his inheritors’ is the source’s wording, not an independently adjudicated legal ruling.

entries.english: Seventh, he realises that the Real’s ruling and self-disclosures in his existence and choices at every time and in every state are specific to that time and state. Judging them to continue unchanged arises from the veil of likeness: the veiled person takes what is now established to be the very thing that has vanished, whereas it is its likeness, not its identity. For this reason we say that self-disclosure does not repeat itself. Yet the divine wont has proceeded by accommodating the veil and its people, out of solicitude for the greater majority. They have become accustomed to it and have judged accordingly. The ruling of the divine instant and task pervades those bound by them necessarily, not by their choice. The possessor of this taste does not judge either of the other two times by something belonging to the past, present or future. Rather, he says: ‘What has passed is gone; what is hoped for is unseen. Yours is the hour in which you are.’
entries.notes: على الآخرين is understood as ‘the other two [times]’, following past/present/future. The concluding verse is unattributed here.

entries.english: As explained earlier, he is the child of his moment, which is his breath (nafas, with a fatḥa on the fāʾ). This is before realisation of the station of perfection. Otherwise, he becomes the father of breaths, states, times, spirits, forms, abodes and other things: all these arise from him, and through him become determined and manifest.

Eighth, he does not mix the ruling of one degree with another: the disciple should obey and the one sought should be obeyed, not conversely. In sum, he ascribes the ruling of each reality to that reality, not another, and every particular to its universal, according to the differentiation in Knowledge which the possessor of this taste witnesses in the Presence of Knowledge. For when the one Being extends over realities and degrees through its Oneness and its comprehensive unitary orientation and requirement—but according to each of those tasks and the Names determined through them—rulings follow only in accordance with the differentiation between them in Knowledge and its concomitants.

Someone who witnesses this as it is will not be veiled by the ruling of the one Being from witnessing the original differentiation. He will not confuse the rulings of the degrees, but know them and their detailed concomitants, and thus judge correctly. For this he needs presence, which is the governing principle of the matter, after knowing that with which he is present among things known and witnessed. He must be certain that presence with everything, like heedlessness of everything, is impossible. Their ruling is therefore determined according to what knowledge appropriate to the time, state, abode, temperament and degree determines, when any of these outweighs what occasions heedlessness. In every state there is presence from one aspect and absence from another. Everyone present is absent, and conversely.

Presence is the clear apprehension of intelligibles and the encompassing of sensibles through the gathered effects of knowledge and witnessing in their possessor, according to the bond between him and them. Its fruits include distinguishing the rulings of the outward revealed Law, the inward Path, the vantage point of Reality, and Oneness beyond that vantage point—each in its own degree and for its own people—for whoever is assisted by God’s immense grace.

The fifth section of this chapter contains a precious governing rule of general benefit to beginner and adept alike.
entries.notes: The fifth-section heading occurs inside the source unit and is retained as a separate paragraph. مطلع is rendered ‘vantage point’, retaining its distinction from what lies beyond it.

entries.english: It explains freedom from the aforementioned confusion and calls attention to presence with realities, with what belongs specifically to the divine rank and what is attributed to the cosmic rank. Its substance, together with what has already been transmitted more than once, is this: every person—indeed, every existent—has an essential relation to the divine rank and a cosmic relation insofar as it is other than God and part of the world. Every matter proceeding from it through acquisition, or coming upon it without acquisition, likewise has these two relations. Everyone should therefore remain present to what belongs specifically to each rank in himself, in what proceeds from him and in what comes upon him, assigning each relation purely to its proper rank. He must not contrive the attribution of a ruling to a rank by arbitrary judgement, so that its effect enters external conduct and he acts upon that contrived attribution. Rather, he must beware of contrivance absolutely, in every matter and state, evil and good—except from the two ranks of revealed Law and nature, speaking with their tongues and acting with their hands. From their standpoint deliberate effort is permitted, but without losing awareness of his realised original relation to the unitary divine rank. Otherwise, there is no difference between this traveller or supposed knower and someone acquainted only with the outward Law.

An example of assigning the two relations purely to their two ranks within oneself is to attribute existence, and the perfections following upon it—the root of knowledge and power, everything involving efficacy, and freedom from deficiencies and vices—to Divinity. One thereby protects oneself through God against claiming any kind of lordship. One fruit is realising our saying: there is no turning away from disobedience to God, and no strength for obedience to Him—indeed, for anything involving efficacy or good—except through God’s granting success. One attributes privative possibility, its aspects of deficiency and vice, and everything belonging to the rank of possibility, such as obedience, servanthood, incapacity and ignorance, to one’s cosmic being. One thereby protects the divine side through oneself against ascribing to Him any aspect of servanthood or blemish. The person truly possessed of taqwā thus combines both relations.
entries.notes: The source exploits the protective sense of taqwā/ittiqāʾ: protecting oneself through God and protecting the divine side through oneself. The clause وجوه الامكان عن النقائص is textually awkward and remains uncorrected in Arabic.

entries.english: An example of assigning these two relations to their ranks in actions that proceed from someone is striking an orphan: if for divinely prescribed discipline, it is rewarded; if for creaturely torment, it is punished. Prescribed acts of obedience and recognised good works done for God’s sake are rewarded. If done to be seen, or so that one may be called generous, a reciter, an ascetic, a scholar, a fighter or a worshipper, they bring no reward but punishment, as transmitted in the report.
entries.notes: Historical disciplinary example translated as the author’s example, not contemporary practical advice. The cited report is not independently authenticated here.

entries.english: Related to this is the difference between one who emigrates for God and His Messenger and the emigrant for Umm Qays. An example of contriving a judgement and acting upon it is believing that charitable works bring reward even when paid for with unlawful wealth, and therefore performing the pilgrimage with it. It has been reported that when such a person says, ‘At Your service, at Your service’, he is answered: ‘No acceptance of your service, and no assistance for you.’ It has also been said: ‘I heard you build a mosque from an exaction, yet, praise be to God, success is not granted you: like one who feeds the hungry from the earnings of her private parts, becoming a proverb for the treacherous giver of charity. The people of understanding and piety told her: “Woe to you: neither fornicate nor give such charity.”’
entries.notes: The report and satirical verses are preserved as cited. جباية may refer to collected revenues or an exaction; the preceding unlawful-wealth example governs the translation.

entries.english: Unqualified contrivance contains a claim to power, which is lordship. It must therefore be avoided altogether, since lordship belongs specifically to Divinity. The Exalted says: ‘God warns you of Himself’ (Qurʾān 3:28). But there is no harm in effort from the rank of the revealed Law: striving to fulfil commands and enjoin them, avoiding prohibitions and forbidding them, with good wisdom and then disputation, according to one’s capacity, by hand, tongue and heart. Nor is there harm in effort from the rank of nature, such as seeking sufficient provision for oneself and one’s dependants. This must be accompanied by awareness that it is done because God has commanded, recommended or permitted it. With this consideration, even eating, drinking or intercourse is rewarded, as the sound report states. The Shaykh indicated this in his Qurʾānic commentary.
entries.notes: حسب الطاعة is interpreted provisionally as ‘according to one’s capacity’ in context; the witness itself is retained. The source expressly permits effort to meet bodily and family needs.

entries.english: We now say: Such a person extracts from every gathering—essential, attributive or active; spiritual or natural; prescribed or customary—what belongs specifically to each of the cosmic and divine realities from which the gathering’s ruling, spirit and form appear, attaching each branch to its root. He is free of the aforementioned confusion and has realised the station of sincerity over which Satan has no authority. Its root is freeing the ruling of Oneness—the rank of your Lord Most High, whose Name you have been commanded to glorify—from the ruling of multiplicity with which every creaturely thing is coloured, whether worshipper or worship. For this secret, the takbīr is prescribed when passing between the states of ritual prayer. Prayer gathers diverse tasks encompassing inward spiritual and outward bodily orientation, in speech and action, in the human rank, then the animal, then the vegetal, until it leads to witnessing with God in the state of the tashahhud. Hence it became the believer’s ascent. For the takbīr means declaring Him free of restriction by differing directions and transformations, by the determinations of knowledge and belief that vary with the degrees, and by every other outward or inward confinement. Thus every takbīr in prayer means: God is too great to be restricted by these transformations of servanthood and cosmic degrees.
entries.notes: The original footnote numerals attached to the human, animal and vegetal ranks are retained in Arabic; their explanatory contents have not been supplied from an unseen apparatus.

entries.english: We now turn to the secret of requiring unity of orientation and freedom from confusion in every intention through which its object is attained, even supplication. In his commentary on the report, the Shaykh explains that the meaning of its being answered is unity of orientation, outwardly and inwardly, together with bringing the requested matter fully to mind. This will be discussed later, God willing.

Know that each individual among outward and inward existents, considered in itself, is only one. The one can be confronted only by another one like itself, and can be joined only to its unitary root, while what resembles it in oneness and in branching from that root is likewise joined to that root. This principle encompasses both the return of each individual to its single species and the return of each species to its single genus.

As for species, it is the complete reality of each individual. As for genus, it is the entirety of the share belonging to each species, and return to the genus concerns that share. Since confrontation, alignment and conjunction occur only between things alike in unity, consider directing a single intention, such as supplication, toward two things resembling one another in branching from one root; or directing a single act, such as prayer, toward two things, such as worship and ostentation; or seeking through that intention or act, precisely in its unity, two purposes, worldly and otherworldly, as in the examples already given. The same applies if you attribute one branch to two roots, just as if you attribute it to a root other than its own: for example, directing one of the five foregoing aspects toward two of them or toward something other than its own root; intending to act according to both your spiritual and bodily constitution at once, as in ablution intended both for drawing near to God and for cooling oneself; or attributing one part to two wholes, as when you attribute your degree simultaneously to the Presence of Necessity and the Presence of Possibility insofar as they are two, rather than from the standpoint of the Cloud or the station of unitary gathering that unites them—
entries.notes: The conditional sentence continues into §4.984. The witness’s بل من حيث appears to require the contrast ‘rather than from the standpoint’; that syntactic interpretation is provisional and Arabic is unchanged. The discussion concerns unified spiritual intention, not an independently established legal invalidation of ablution.

entries.english: —then the satanic ruling enters upon you, and sincerity belonging to the All-Merciful is removed through dispersal of aspiration, fragmentation of gatheredness, confusion between incompatible rulings, and alteration of the comprehensive seeking orientation through deviation from alignment in certain respects. You are deprived of sound knowledge that distinguishes every reality together with its rulings, and thus deprived of harvesting the fruit of your knowledge—which is complete orientation—namely, attainment of what is sought.

As the Shaykh says in his commentary on the report: ‘After the aforementioned unity of orientation, the answer follows one’s conception. The person whose conception of the Real is soundest has his supplications answered. Sound conception depends upon realised knowledge and sound witnessing, as he said, peace and blessings be upon him and his family: “If you knew God as He ought to be known, mountains would move through your supplication.” These are the people promised an answer in His saying: “Call upon Me; I shall answer you” (Qurʾān 40:60). For someone who does not know has not called upon the Real, and so He does not answer him.’ Here his words end.
entries.notes: The mountain-moving report is translated as cited, with no claim to independent authentication. The quotation’s account of answered prayer is preserved as its author’s argument.

entries.english: When God supports you by inspiring avoidance of what has been mentioned, so that this unity of orientation is realised, together with mastery of the preceding principles establishing the Oneness of the One toward whom you turn—through realised experiential knowledge, not theoretical knowledge behind the veil of speculation or ambiguous knowledge by imitation—you will be safe from confusion and dispersal. Satan will submit at your hand through his inability to divert you from the direction of the One, the Unique. Your state and affair will lead you to receive everything that comes upon you from its proper source and in the manner in which it comes, from whatever degree and through whatever intermediary locus of manifestation it arrives, or through the self-disclosure of the particular face, in which there is no intermediary and which has no determination.

As for loci of manifestation—whether they are conditions completing the recipient’s preparedness to receive the Real’s effect, as we hold, or intermediaries conveying His effect, as the speculative thinkers hold, which is why they have not recognised the effect of the particular face—they may arise from the orientation itself. This is a matter proceeding from it whose effect returns upon it in a manner other than that in which it proceeded; this is indicated by His saying: ‘Evil plotting encompasses only its own people’ (Qurʾān 35:43). Or they may arise from something else. If that other belongs to the Presence of meanings, it is the contemplated, determinate Name among God’s Names. If it belongs to the Presence of spirits, it is a reality of the spiritual kingdom: the purely good is an angel, the purely evil a devil, and what moves between the two is a jinn. If it belongs to the Presence of images, it is the reality giving imaginal form; if to delimited imagination, it is the reality assuming imagined form. Imagination may produce an effect that intellection does not, as is explained in Ibn Sīnā’s al-Ishārāt.
entries.notes: الممثلة / المتمثلة are distinguished as giving versus assuming imaginal form, provisionally pending vocalised or printed collation. The referent of ‘from the orientation itself’ is compressed in the Arabic.

entries.english: If it belongs to the sensory world, it is either human or otherwise. In the human case, it is either the person himself—whether spiritualised, like al-Khiḍr and Jesus, peace be upon them, or not spiritualised—or the power of his orientation, namely his projected aspiration. As the saying goes: ‘The aspiration of men uproots mountains.’ In ordinary language, himma is a kind of intention; technically, it is the seeking impulse arising from souls and spirits toward objects of perfection and ultimate purposes. It varies with the kinds of people who possess it and with differences in their apprehensions and degrees.
Some direct their aspiration toward worldly matters, whose principal kinds are mentioned in His saying: ‘Made attractive to people is the love of desires—for women …’ (Qurʾān 3:14).
Others direct their aspiration toward the hereafter and spiritual perfections: ‘The hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in distinction’ (Qurʾān 17:21).

Others attach their aspiration to what is with God and in God: ‘For this let those who compete compete’ (Qurʾān 83:26). They differ according to their shares from God and their stations and degrees of perfection and greater perfection.

Whichever of these a person’s aspiration attaches to becomes his ultimate object, and the limit of his attainment, if it is decreed for him. The most perfect among them attaches his aspiration to nothing but the pure Real, without turning in passionate love toward any of the things mentioned. Thus al-Jandī said.

As for what is not human, it is a higher celestial power drawn toward its recipient through a spiritual relation and an affinity with that sphere required by the determination of his spirit; or through a relation of nativity required, inwardly, by the ascendant at the implantation of his seed and, outwardly, by the ascendant at his birth. All this concerns these factors individually.
entries.notes: The astrological account is translated as historical source doctrine; no empirical validity is asserted.

entries.english: As for their combinations, these comprise either all of them or some of them, with the ruling of the self-disclosure of the particular face joined to the whole. These exhaust the paths of divine descents, lordly incoming inspirations, diverse receptions and distinct impartations: nothing falls outside this governing rule.

Know that the prescribed form of supplication indicates unity of orientation in the sense explained. The Shaykh says in his commentary on the report: ‘One hand expresses the supplicant’s outward dimension, the other his inward dimension, and the tongue his entirety. Wiping the face indicates return to the reality combining spirit and body, an allusion to his immutable entity in the Real’s Knowledge from eternity. For a thing’s face is its reality, and this face manifests that reality. Through this the meaning of “Everything perishes except His face” (Qurʾān 28:88) becomes known, as does another secret that cannot be divulged.’ Here his words end.

The sixth section of this chapter, explaining the orientation of love.
entries.notes: The section heading is part of the source unit. The passage supplies a symbolic reading of gestures of supplication; their legal status is not independently adjudicated here.

entries.english: This is the first connection between the lordly relation belonging to the Reality of realities—as explained in the meaning of ‘I loved to be known’—and cosmic recipients. It impels the aforementioned manifestation and concerns the perfection of disclosure and self-contemplation attained through the Perfect Human after the manifestation of his existential parts, upon which the manifestation of the whole depends. Because both sides share the function of a mirror, this connection pervades every existent. From the Real’s side it is the seeking of the manifestation of the Essence and the perfections of the Names through action and influence; from the cosmos’s side, the seeking of the manifestation of rulings and states through being affected and receiving. This will be established in discussing al-Nafaḥāt, God willing. Several preliminaries will explain secrets of this chapter not treated in the exposition of His saying: ‘He is the Forgiving, the Loving’ (Qurʾān 85:14).
entries.notes: جلاء / استجلاء are distinguished as disclosure and self-contemplation or seeing clearly in a mirror. ‘I loved to be known’ is translated as the source’s quotation, not authenticated as a prophetic report.

entries.english: First: orientation and anticipation—that is, adorning and preparing oneself to seek—as well as seeking and such related things as inclination, passionate love, desire, requirement and will, are all love’s impulses and impartations: its impartations insofar as they impel toward love’s object, which is union and the removal of the difference that produces estrangement. The expressions differ because the school of realisation does not admit synonymy, their degrees and determinate rulings differing according to the persons in whom those rulings appear. Times, through states—that is, the divine instant and task—determine the forms of particular preparednesses in concrete existence. They indicate their possessor’s rank, sometimes through the particular determinate state and sometimes through the essence under the ruling of universal preparedness. The differences between these expressions thus turn upon relational considerations that are love’s subtle threads and its determinations according to the states and preparednesses of lovers.

Second: love as such does not attach to something already possessed, since seeking what is already obtained is impossible. It attaches to something absent, in the seeker’s estimation, at the time of seeking, even if that thing exists in itself and in relation to another. The Essence of the Real can therefore be sought or loved only by the Perfect Human, or by the rare individuals who share this taste with the perfected ones. For every existent takes unqualified existence to be already attained, knowing that attainment immediately, and so does not seek it. The Perfect Human, or someone sharing his taste, seeks it with regard to its unrestricted rank of perfection or greater perfection. This is not already attained, even though unqualified existence is attained. A thing taken without qualification differs from that thing considered in its unrestrictedness; contemplating and seeking unrestrictedness is conceivable only for someone fitted for it. For those other than the Perfect Human and those sharing his taste, the object of love is not the Real’s Essence but something from the Real that has not been attained: witnessing Him, continuous witnessing, proximity, knowledge, or some religious or worldly felicity in the form of states, stations, purposes and restricted degrees. In sum, it is attaining what suits the spirit, such as knowledge and witnessing, or the temperament, or both, whether through its acquisition, completion or permanence; or removing what is unsuitable, according to the same distinctions. The unsuitable thing exists, but its removal has not been attained. These objects are called relative perfections.
entries.notes: The passage hinges on مطلق الشيء versus الشيء من حيث ملاحظة إطلاقه: a thing taken without qualification versus that thing expressly considered in its unrestrictedness. The English retains this distinction.

entries.english: He says in al-Nafaḥāt: ‘In the perspective of realisation, it is impossible for something to love what is other than itself precisely insofar as it differs from it. Veiled people imagine that the Real loves His servants, or that some among them love Him, precisely insofar as they differ from Him, taking this from “He loves them and they love Him” (Qurʾān 5:54), “He loves the patient” (3:146), and “He loves those who do good” (2:195). Rather, this occurs through the ruling of a meaning shared between them. Through that meaning an affinity is established which requires the predominance of what unites over what distinguishes and separates. Through knowledge or awareness of that affinity, the knower or perceiver seeks the complete removal of the rulings of separation and the manifestation of the sovereignty of what unites, so that complete connection may be realised and the sovereignty of the One, the Unique, appear. It is therefore not admissible that the Real should love creation, or conversely [insofar as they differ]. Rather, there are other secrets—essential, attributive, active, pertaining to states or to degrees—through which affinity is established and love arises. Apart from this it is not admissible.’ Thus far his words.
entries.notes: The bracketed qualification is demanded by the quotation’s opening and Fanārī’s explicit explanation in §4.1000; the source does not deny all love between God and creation.

entries.english: This does not mean that there is no love whatsoever between the Real and creation, or no essential love at all. It means that love does not occur insofar as they differ. Insofar as they have an affinity through one of the five aspects, the five preceding kinds of love are realised. The explanation of love from both sides will follow, God willing.

Third: objects of seeking have two roots, cosmic and lordly. Cosmic objects—that is, what cosmic realities seek—are of several kinds: natural but not elemental; elemental; spiritual and clothed in a form; or unclothed, being immaterial meanings within the rank of possibility. Lordly objects—that is, those toward which the comprehensive divine Reality turns—are either existential determinations in loci of manifestation or universal unseen determinations of the Names.

Fourth: nothing seeks another without a comprehensive affinity between them. This is any unifying factor in whose ruling and effect they participate alike, sharing it in a way that removes multiplicity between them—not absolutely, but insofar as each corresponds to that unifying factor with a correspondence leaving no difference, and insofar as they resemble one another in their share of it and its effect. From the standpoint of these things’ union with the unifying factor, its ruling is theirs: what is affirmed of them is affirmed of it, and what is denied of them is denied of it. Their difference, however, belongs to the particularities by which they are distinguished.

Fifth: as previously transmitted from the commentary on the report concerning His saying, ‘He is the Forgiving, the Loving’ (Qurʾān 85:14), the subtle connecting thread through which affinity’s ruling flows sometimes arises from one side and sometimes from both. It divides into orientation through the servant’s wayfaring and descent from the Lord. Their meeting is then called a mutual encounter if it occurs in the middle; descent if the lordly movement passes beyond the middle; and drawing near if the traveller passes beyond it. The fruit of all these is the manifestation of the perfection dependent upon that meeting, through joining the branch to its root and completing the whole through the part.
entries.notes: Technical sequence: منازلة (mutual encounter), تدلّي (descent), تداني (drawing near). The directional account explicates the source’s compressed clauses بعد تجاوزه الرباني / بعد التجاوز من السالك.

entries.english: Once you understand these preliminaries, know that the Shaykh explains in al-Nafaḥāt that love is a unitary reality of seeking whose ruling is shared by the divine and cosmic ranks because of an established affinity between the Real and creation. It can accordingly be attributed to the Real from one aspect and to creation likewise, through that affinity, which we shall explain further, God willing. Its causes are multiple.

Among them are the attributes of the two who love one another and their union through those attributes, even though their shares in them differ. For the ruling of an attribute cannot appear in two loci in precisely the same way: there must be disparity, because the preparednesses of unmade quiddities differ, requiring reception of the one Being in diverse modes and in the forms of varied shares. For this reason likeness between two things in every respect cannot be found, and self-disclosure does not repeat itself.
entries.notes: The witness’s punctuation separates منها after تفاوت حظوظهما; the translation joins it to the preceding phrase (‘their shares in them’) without altering the Arabic.

entries.english: If you object: ‘Unity is an essential attribute of the Real, and multiplicity an essential attribute of the world. Their attributes therefore oppose one another, rather than having affinity.’

I reply: But it has already been explained that the truth is that unity has a relational multiplicity: one is conceived as half of two, a third of three, and so forth. These are conceptual considerations that produce no multiplicity in the essence. All divine attributes must be understood in this way. Multiplicity, in turn, has its own unity: the unity of the intelligibility of the aggregate insofar as it is an aggregate and a whole. Whenever either knows the other, or a connection between them is conceived, this occurs through the ruling of what they share. This one knows that one only through what it contains of it. Thus the Shaykh said.

He also says there: ‘Love between two may result from participation and affinity in certain states, acts or degrees—for example, participation in prophethood, sainthood, vicegerency, or essential knowledge of God or of something else. For us, knowledge may be essential and thus not counted as an attribute.’

He says there: ‘The explanation that unveils the secret of the beloved’s love for the lover and the lover’s love for the beloved is that the beloved loves the lover because the lover is a means for contemplating his perfection and a locus in which the sovereignty of his beauty is exercised. The lover is the beloved’s mirror, in which he clearly beholds his own beauties hidden within his unity. Excessive proximity and being alone had veiled him from them. When he beholds them in another, through the occurrence of a certain multiplicity and distinction, he loves them with a love impossible without that mirror.’

Moreover, the comprehensive copy of human reality contains both what deserves to be loved with all love and what produces aversion relative to opposed realities. When a mirror becomes determined in which what deserves love is distinguished—whether an attribute, act, state, or something containing all or some of these—and the veil of excessive proximity is lifted, love’s sovereignty appears, seeking to remove the rulings of multiplicity and otherness by giving predominance to what unites over what distinguishes. Thus one loves oneself in what differs from oneself in one respect, through the essential attribute within oneself that seeks perfect disclosure and self-contemplation. This attribute is what calls for the world’s creation; creation’s purpose is nothing other than this. Every other stated purpose of creation is a branch of, and subordinate to, perfect disclosure and self-contemplation. This ruling pervades every lover, although the aspects and considerations differ. Yet the lover’s contemplation and the beloved’s contemplation differ in several ways.

One difference is that the beloved is a mirror of the lover’s essence insofar as he is a lover. In that mirror he beholds himself, and secondarily some of his own beauties. The lover, however, is the mirror of the perfection of the beloved’s beauty and the locus in which the rulings of his sovereignty operate. This ruling pervades every lover and beloved without exception, and the Real’s relation to His creation is of this kind.

In our realities—that is, the forms of our being known, fixed in His Knowledge—we are mirrors of His absolute, essential, unitary Being. For He is Being itself, and none besides Him has being; thus He beholds Himself in us. His Presence, however, is a mirror of our manifold states and multiplicities. We apprehend only one another, but in the Real. What is loved on our side is what we behold in Him, which is nothing but attributes and states. He loves Himself in us, since seeing Himself in a mirror that differs from Him in one respect differs from seeing Himself in Himself for Himself. Indeed, there there is neither seeing nor number. For the differing mirror, as the locus of a self-disclosure restricted by it, determines in what is imprinted upon it a ruling that was not determined when He saw Himself [in Himself]. Whoever apprehends this secret knows the secret of Essence, attributes, states, mirrors and loci of disclosure, and knows that the world, with its realities and forms, is a mirror of the Real from one aspect, while the Real is a mirror of the world from another.
entries.notes: The witness reads فيحب منا; the passive sense ‘what is loved on our side’ is adopted provisionally. The explicitly qualified respects of mirroring are preserved.

entries.english: These words accord with his repeatedly cited statement: ‘You are His mirror, and He is the mirror of your states.’ Our saying ‘He is your mirror’ is also valid insofar as your reality is one of His states. Likewise, ‘You are the mirror of His tasks, attributes and Names’ is valid insofar as concomitants are concomitants of the Essence.

We now say: Seekers among the servants are of two kinds, knowing and unknowing. The unknowing person’s intercessor is affinity and connection through the essential subtle thread. The one who knows the foregoing secrets has the support both of affinity and of knowledge, which shortens the distance and severs attachments and obstacles preventing the completion of affinity’s form and the strengthening of its ruling. Assistance and support strengthen the shared measure through each individual reality contained within the essences of seeker and sought, together with their concomitants. This is indicated by the saying, peace and blessings be upon him and his family: ‘Assume the character traits of God.’ To this category also belongs his saying to the Companion who asked to be his companion in Paradise: ‘Help me concerning yourself through abundant prostration.’ This was to acquire affinity and participation with him by constant adherence to the realities of worship. This is an exceedingly precious taste. Whoever apprehends its secret knows the secret of actions universally: their diversity results from differences in the realities of those through whom the acts of entities appear, and the secret of affinity is observed in them all so that the fruit may be realised and the purpose completed.

The seventh section of this chapter, concerning the secret of the orientation called supplication, its rulings, and the principles of its concomitants.
entries.notes: The source attributes both sayings to the Prophet; no equal claim to hadith authenticity is inferred. The seventh-section heading is retained within its numbered unit.

entries.english: Know that supplication and asking require an impulse, namely poverty and need; an aim, namely obtaining what is needed; that from which the need arises; an orientation through which seeking and requesting occur; a tongue for requesting and seeking; and a response from the Real through which the needed object is attained. These are six matters, each of which must be examined with its divisions.

The first, need, may be essential or attributive. In either case, what is needed must be appropriate to it. Essential need seeks essential gifts, that is, gifts attributed to the essence of Divinity: distinctive self-disclosures from God in the unity that gathers all divine Names, a comprehensive unity particular to the most perfect of those brought near and the rare perfected individuals. For the Essence simply as such neither gives nor discloses itself in any self-disclosure. Attributive need seeks gifts of the Names, from the individual Presences of the Names according to the recipient’s receptivity and particular state: his orientation as dependent upon his knowledge, belief, temperament, psychic condition and bodily natural condition, and whatever predominates in the combination of these and in what it produces at the time of asking. Either kind of asking—arising from essential or attributive need—may be verbal. Verbal asking may specify its object, as when you say, ‘My Lord, give me such-and-such’, or leave it unspecified, as when you say, ‘My Lord, give me what is beneficial for me’, whether either request seeks existence or suitable perfections.
entries.notes: The source explicitly excludes giving and self-disclosure from the Essence qua Essence. معَيِّن is active here (‘specifying’), distinguished from the passive form in §4.1017.

entries.english: The second is the aim. As explained, it is either specified or unspecified: simply the seeker’s attainment of what he needs for his existence, if the gift is essential, or of the causes sustaining his existence, if it is attributive. Either seeks the perfection he can attain, whatever it may be: whether consciously perceived or not, natural, psychic, spiritual, intellectual or lordly, among the kinds of requesting to be explained.

The third is that from which seeking arises. If the object is unspecified, seeking it is the ruling of the comprehensive Reality pervading the seeker through its Oneness. If specified, its specification arises from the predominant ruling of certain realities and human constituents contained within the human essence. The kinds of requesting thus correspond to the powers, realities and rulings of degrees contained within the seeker’s essence and constitution. Through that particular constitution he can manifest those degrees and gather those powers and realities in the state of seeking, gathering, and comprehensive or differentiated manifestation.

Since the human being is a copy gathering every matter and a form encompassing everything in meaning, form and rank, the divine orientation that brings him into existence requires him to have a seeking appropriate to every degree. His requests are accordingly of several kinds: natural, psychic, spiritual, intellectual, and purely lordly, abstracted from all materials. Divine incoming inspirations, commands, prohibitions, self-disclosures and all other objects of seeking occur in accordance with these. Everything contains everything, although we may not know it. What is opposed does not receive what is inappropriate to it or know it from its unknown and opposed aspect, because there is no unifying factor. This may arise from a psychic condition. Thus, if a spiritual matter comes to someone in a natural state, it comes at the request of a hidden spiritual thread latent within him without his awareness; he therefore disclaims, rejects and denies it. The same applies to someone in a spiritual or intellectual state.
entries.notes: The sequence لكنه قد لا نعلم … قد يكون من الحال النفساني is syntactically unstable. The translation preserves its account of unnoticed affinities without supplying an absent doctrinal premise.

entries.english: Corresponding to each person in what we have described is a particular relation whose ruling is determined by the servant’s particular receptivity and his concrete preparedness in that state. This relation determined from God is what is expressed by the Name particular to that incoming inspiration or self-disclosure.

Among these are the self-disclosures of transcendence and likeness, and the rejection and denial occurring in the world. Through this one understands that self-disclosures are relatively general or particular, all according to the degrees of those requesting, the states of seekers and their preparednesses. This is what he says in his Qurʾānic commentary: ‘Every supplication proceeding from a supplicant through one of the tongues has, corresponding to it from the root of the rank on which it rests according to the supplicant’s knowledge or belief, an answer which the supplicant calls forth through that tongue, determined by the state and attribute predominant in him when he supplicates.’ Here his words end.

We now say: The seeker either seeks from the standpoint of knowing and being present with what he seeks, or not from that standpoint. In the first case there are two possibilities. If at some time he is granted the witnessing of his reality together with the entities necessarily accompanying it, as all of them are in God’s Knowledge eternally, he then knows what will be determined for him from them in this constitution and in whatever worlds God wills. He gains an encompassing view of what his essence contains, in a general way with some detail. Yet this apprehension, precious as it is and rare as its possessors are, lasts only briefly and cannot endure continuously, for a secret that cannot be explained, although it may be indicated later.

I say: Perhaps this is because continuous, enduring comprehensiveness belongs specifically to the Real, as has already been explained to you. Or perhaps it points to what will come at the book’s end: among the signs of someone travelling through the degrees of greater perfection is that he knows a thing as though he did not know it—indeed, he is that very thing as though he were not it.

Among the reasons for this are the secret of his gatheredness and unity and the non-persistence of what is imprinted upon his mirror. Things circle his reality, which is the centre of their circle. Each aligns with him for one breath, then passes beyond that alignment in the next. No point of a relation or of a cosmic reality can remain at the position of alignment without another point following it in a state different from the first. This continues perpetually. Its explanation, together with answers to objections, will be given there.

The possessor of this tongue is therefore generally clear-sighted concerning his states, receiving them through witnessing confirmed by prior knowledge, whether they suit him or not, and whether they are good or bad in people’s eyes or in the reality of the matter itself. Knowing that there is no escape from them, he supplicates only for them, whether the answer accompanies the request or is delayed. Most of his supplications, in their various aforementioned kinds, are answered, because his unveiling prevents him from asking except for what must occur on condition of asking, or what may occur. This latter applies in two situations: first, where the matter has not yet been differentiated for him, but its knowledge has been given generally; second, where causes of rejection and withholding have been left in place for him. Among the states he sees, he sees the form of supplication accompanied by withholding, yet cannot refrain from or repel it. As explained, he knows that he cannot escape it and that unveiling prevents him from not asking.
entries.notes: فيما لم ينفصل عنه بعد is interpreted as a matter not yet differentiated or clarified for him, in contrast with أجمل له علمه; this reading remains provisional.

entries.english: The causes of rejection are left in place for him for two reasons. First is the secret of following his Lord, who does not appear in every aspect in every locus, just as He appears in a given aspect only in a locus receptive to it. This is the secret of the comprehensive Reality’s combining acceptance and withholding according to the loci of manifestation. As established in the Qurʾānic commentary, pains and other disagreeable things befall the perfected ones because they manifest the station of gathering. Second is the secret of servanthood’s lowliness and lordship’s exaltation, required by the established aspect of possibility. In the perfected person, a ruling and effect of both aspects must appear.

Do you not see the secret and indication of this in the most perfect Muḥammadan station and its most complete and just balance? He said, ‘I do not know what will be done with me or with you’ (Qurʾān 46:9), although he possessed clear insight from his Lord. He also said, ‘You know better the affairs of your world’, although he reported the advance signs of the Mahdī that would come after six hundred and some years; similar examples have already been given. All this concerns the supplicant granted the witnessing of his reality.
entries.notes: The dating of the Mahdī’s signs is the source’s historical claim and has not been verified or endorsed. Qurʾānic and reported statements are translated in the author’s argumentative context.

entries.english: If, however, the supplicant’s moment requires worship under the ruling of a particular station and determinate rank—which is most commonly the case—his seeking accords with that rank, state, constitution or other restrictions that serve, wholly or partly, as conditions. All this concerns seeking of which he has knowledge and awareness. Considered through his essence and comprehensive constitution, however, in every breath he seeks from the Real, for every reality contained within his constitution at the moment of seeking, that by which the manifestation of its rulings persists, that by which the Real appears through it, and that through which and in which its perfection is attained, together with the concomitants of the aforementioned restrictions.

The fourth is the orientation through which seeking occurs. It may be unitary, comprising sound conception and perfect following, or otherwise. As he says in al-Nuṣūṣ: ‘The sounder a person’s knowledge and conception of the Real, the swifter the answer concerning the very thing requested. The more completely he watches over the Real’s commands and hastens to fulfil them with perfect compliance, the more completely the Real complies with him.’ For this reason most supplications of the great ones are answered. This is indicated by: ‘Call upon Me; I shall answer you’ (Qurʾān 40:60).

Someone without knowledge, whose conception is unsound, is not calling upon the Real who guaranteed an answer. He is turning toward a particularised form in his mind, produced by his own reflection, imagination, another’s state and reflection, or a combination of these. Hence the answer is withheld or delayed. Whenever such a person is answered, the cause is the secret of divine accompaniment or the complete gatheredness attained by those in desperate need, who have been promised an answer because of the preparedness produced by their distress. Someone with a sound conception brings the Real to presence and turns toward Him with realised presence and orientation. This need not be from every aspect: it suffices to be present with Him in certain degrees and through certain Names and attributes. This is the state of those midway among the people of God; the former is the state of the veiled. Thus far his words. We shall transmit the account of the perfected ones’ orientation in its proper place.

He says in his Qurʾānic commentary: ‘Sound conception and attentive bringing-to-presence have a great effect upon the answer. The Prophet took this into account and urged it upon ʿAlī when teaching him the supplication containing “O God, guide me and make me straight.” He told him: “Recall by your guidance the guidance of the road, and by straightness the straightness of an arrow.” He thus instructed him to bring these two things to mind while supplicating.’

‘Whoever conceives correctly the One he calls upon and asks, through reflection and knowledge preceding or present at the supplication, and then calls upon Him—especially after His command to supplicate and His undertaking to answer—will assuredly be answered. Someone who claims to call Zayd while bringing someone else to mind, and then receives no answer, should blame only himself. Yet his request may bear fruit through the intercession of his good opinion of his Lord and through divine accompaniment and encompassing presence. Someone mistaken in his orientation is therefore right from one aspect, like a mistaken practitioner of independent judgement: rewarded, not altogether deprived.’ Here his words end.

The fifth is the tongues of supplication and seeking. One is the outward tongue—‘by which I mean form’, he says in the commentary—namely the tongue of spoken expression. Another is the inward tongue, which is other than this. Seeking occurs through both or through either. Yet the outward tongue is never without some subtle threads of the inward, while the inward tongue is not bound by the outward’s restriction, although it is not free of connection with it, of the outward’s expressing it, or of the ruling of the station and state under which it falls. As for the inward tongue—
entries.notes: السنة is read as ألسنة, ‘tongues’, as confirmed by the enumeration. The sentence continues into §4.1034.

entries.english: —he says in the commentary that it may be the tongue of the spirit, the tongue of the state, the tongue of the station, or the tongue of universal, essential, unseen preparedness, whose ruling pervades through particular existential preparednesses. Here his words end.

In sum, know that the human being has a tongue according to his universal state and his humanity: the comprehensive tongue—indeed, tongues, since it gathers them. The same is true according to his original overall preparedness, every constitution in which he exists, and every form in which he himself appears. Each particular existential preparedness also has a tongue. In every breath he is seeking, sometimes through some of these and sometimes through all; sometimes with knowledge, witnessing, awareness and presence, and sometimes without most or some of these. Sometimes he combines two requests from two aspects, aware of one and unaware of the other. In this combination, the request may require a swift or slow answer from the unknown aspect, while requiring no answer or a delayed answer from the known, intended aspect.
